<reason>Both sides were strong and disciplined, but A built the cleaner path. A defined "more responsibility" in the opening as duties, mandatory insurance, and liability for unused geofencing, then defended that frame throughout. A flipped B's analogies (continuous remote control vs rental handover; dashboard vs bartender), turned "operators will exit cities" into proof that liability shapes operator conduct, and answered both pressure questions with workable mechanisms: rider penalties plus subrogation for deterrence, and a negligence standard anchored to speed caps that need no sidewalk-level GPS precision. The decisive tilt came on compensation: pressed by A's Q1, B adopted an operator-administered insurance pool, which A's closing fairly converted into movement toward the motion ("conceded and renamed"). B landed real blows — the compliance-vs-liability distinction was sharp, and the precision trap forced A off sidewalk-specific detection — but B overstated the resulting "concession," the car-displacement chain stayed asserted rather than demonstrated, and A's kinetic-energy answer neutralized B's "speed, not aim" rebuttal. B was also clipped twice, a real execution cost; A's broken [C2.x] references were a smaller one.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 flipping both of B's analogies (operator never loses control vs rental handover; live dashboard beats the bartender's eyes) and recasting "operators exit cities" as proof liability works — followed by the closing that converted B's pressure-driven no-fault insurance pool into a partial concession of the motion.</best_rebuttal>
